label: Virtual DOM
tooltip: An in-memory representation of the real DOM. React diffs old and new versions to compute the minimal set of DOM updates.
definition: The Virtual DOM is React's in-memory representation of the UI tree. When state changes, React builds a new virtual tree, compares it against the previous one, and applies only the diff to the real DOM. The point is that you can write code as if the whole UI re-renders on every change — React makes it efficient under the hood. This is what allows the declarative model to scale.

label: Reconciliation
tooltip: The algorithm React uses to figure out the minimum DOM operations needed to update the UI when state or props change.
definition: Reconciliation is the algorithm React uses to diff the previous element tree against the new one. It uses two heuristics: different element types produce different trees (so type changes cause unmount/remount), and stable `key` props identify children across renders. Understanding reconciliation is what makes keys, stable component identities, and subtree-remount bugs click into place.

label: Hook
tooltip: A function (useState, useEffect, etc.) that lets function components opt into React features like state, lifecycle, and context.
definition: Hooks are functions starting with `use` that let function components access state, side effects, refs, context, and other React features that used to require class components. Rules: call hooks at the top level (no conditionals), only call them from React functions. The hook system is built on calling order — that's why the rules exist.

label: StrictMode
tooltip: A dev-only wrapper that surfaces problems by double-invoking effects, reducers, and state initialisers.
definition: `<React.StrictMode>` is a development-only wrapper that intentionally double-invokes function component bodies, class render methods, reducers, and state initialisers. It also runs effects through a setup→cleanup→setup cycle to simulate a remount. The point is to catch effects that aren't idempotent — bugs that would otherwise only show up under concurrent rendering. It's a no-op in production.
codeExample:
<React.StrictMode>
  <App />
</React.StrictMode>

label: Hydration
tooltip: The process of attaching React's event handlers and state to server-rendered HTML so the page becomes interactive.
definition: When the server sends pre-rendered HTML, the browser shows it immediately — but it isn't interactive yet. Hydration is the process where React downloads the JS bundle, walks the DOM, and attaches event handlers, restores state, and connects the rendered HTML to its component tree. A hydration mismatch happens when the server-rendered output doesn't match what the client would render — usually caused by reading `window`, `Date.now()`, or other non-deterministic values during render.

label: Generic
tooltip: A type parameter that lets a function or type work with multiple input types while preserving the relationship between them.
definition: Generics let you write a function or type that works with multiple input types without losing type information. The classic use is a function whose return type depends on its input: `first<T>(arr: T[]): T | undefined` preserves the element type, so `first([1,2,3])` returns `number | undefined`, not `unknown | undefined`. Generics also work on classes, interfaces, and type aliases.

label: Type Inference
tooltip: The compiler's ability to figure out a type from context, so you don't have to annotate everything by hand.
definition: TypeScript infers types from initialisers, return values, and function calls so you don't have to annotate every variable. `const x = 42` is inferred as `number`. `users.map(u => u.name)` infers `string[]` if `users` is typed. Over-annotating is the rookie move — let the compiler do the work and only annotate at API boundaries (function parameters, exported function returns).

label: Discriminated Union
tooltip: A union type where each variant has a literal property the compiler can use to narrow which variant you're holding.
definition: A discriminated union (or tagged union) is a union type where every member has a shared property holding a unique literal value — the discriminant. The compiler narrows the union based on that discriminant inside conditional checks. This pattern replaces enums + interfaces with something safer and more ergonomic.

label: Structural Typing
tooltip: TypeScript matches types by shape, not by name — duck typing with compiler help.
definition: TypeScript uses structural typing: two types are compatible if they have the same shape, regardless of whether either was declared to implement the other. A plain object literal can satisfy an interface without ever being declared as that interface. This is the opposite of nominal typing in languages like Java or C#.

label: const Assertion
tooltip: `as const` tells TS to infer the narrowest possible type — string literals stay literal, arrays become readonly tuples.
definition: `as const` narrows inference to the most specific type possible. String literals stay as their literal type, arrays become readonly tuples, object properties become readonly literal types. The classic use is deriving a union type from a runtime constant — define the values once, derive the type from `typeof`.

label: App Router
tooltip: Next.js 13+ routing system built on React Server Components, living in the app/ directory.
definition: The App Router is the routing system introduced in Next.js 13 and stabilised in 14. It lives in `app/` and is built on React Server Components by default. Key features: nested layouts that persist across navigation, streaming with Suspense, parallel and intercepting routes, route handlers for APIs, and per-segment loading and error states.
codeExample:
app/
├── layout.tsx     // wraps everything
├── page.tsx       // /
└── blog/
    ├── page.tsx           // /blog
    └── [slug]/
        └── page.tsx       // /blog/:slug

label: Server Component
tooltip: A React component that renders on the server and never ships its JS to the browser. Default in App Router.
definition: A React Server Component renders on the server (at build or request time) and never ships its JavaScript to the browser. It can fetch data directly, read from databases, access environment variables — anything server-side. The browser receives just the rendered HTML / RSC payload. In Next.js App Router, components are Server Components by default; you opt into client behaviour with `'use client'`.

label: ISR
tooltip: Incremental Static Regeneration — serve static pages but refresh them in the background after a time window or on-demand.
definition: ISR (Incremental Static Regeneration) lets you serve statically generated pages but refresh them after a TTL or via on-demand invalidation. You get CDN-speed responses with eventual freshness. Configure with `export const revalidate = N` for time-based refresh, or `revalidatePath` / `revalidateTag` for on-demand invalidation when underlying data changes.

label: Route Handler
tooltip: App Router replacement for API routes. A route.ts file exporting HTTP method functions using standard Web Request/Response.
definition: Route Handlers are the App Router replacement for `pages/api/` routes. A `route.ts` file inside `app/` exports HTTP method functions (`GET`, `POST`, `PATCH`, etc.) that use the standard Web `Request` and `Response` objects rather than Next-specific `req`/`res`. This makes them portable and easier to test.

label: Middleware
tooltip: Code that runs at the Edge before a request reaches a route — used for auth gates, redirects, A/B tests, locale negotiation.
definition: Middleware runs at the Edge before a request hits a route. The function receives a `NextRequest` and returns a `NextResponse` — it can redirect, rewrite, set cookies, or modify request headers. Configure which routes it runs on via a `matcher` config. In Next 16+, the file is named `proxy.ts` (same API). Keep it small — runs on every matched request.

label: Redux Store
tooltip: The single object that holds the entire application state tree in a Redux app.
definition: The Redux store is the single source of truth for application state. Created with `configureStore()` (Redux Toolkit) or the legacy `createStore()`, it exposes three core methods: `getState()` to read the current state, `dispatch(action)` to trigger a state change, and `subscribe(listener)` to react to changes. There is always exactly one store per Redux application — multiple data domains are handled by combining slice reducers, not by creating multiple stores.

label: Reducer
tooltip: A pure function (state, action) => newState that describes how state changes in response to an action.
definition: A reducer is a pure function that takes the current state and an action object and returns the next state — never mutating the original. The name comes from `Array.prototype.reduce`: just as reduce folds an array into a single value, a Redux reducer folds a stream of dispatched actions into the current state. Rules: no side effects, no direct mutations, always return the current state unchanged for unknown action types. Redux Toolkit's `createSlice` generates reducers with Immer baked in, so you can write mutating-looking code that produces new immutable state.

label: Action
tooltip: A plain JS object with a `type` field that describes what happened in the app.
definition: An action is the only way to describe a state change in Redux — a plain object with at minimum a `type` string. By convention (and Redux Toolkit's Flux Standard Action shape) it also carries a `payload` field for data. Actions are dispatched to the store, which passes them through middleware and then to the root reducer. With `createSlice`, action creators are auto-generated and fully typed — you rarely write action objects by hand.

label: Dispatch
tooltip: The store method that sends an action through middleware and into the root reducer to update state.
definition: `store.dispatch(action)` is the only way to trigger a state change. It sends the action through the middleware pipeline (thunk, logger, etc.) and then calls the root reducer with the current state and that action. In React components, use the typed `useAppDispatch` hook rather than importing the store directly — this keeps components decoupled from the store singleton and ensures correct TypeScript inference.

label: Thunk
tooltip: A function dispatched to the Redux store instead of a plain action object, used to handle async logic.
definition: A thunk is a function that wraps an expression to delay its evaluation — in Redux it is a function you dispatch that the `redux-thunk` middleware intercepts before it reaches the reducer. The thunk receives `(dispatch, getState)` and can perform async work (API calls, timeouts) then dispatch plain actions with the results. Redux Toolkit ships `createAsyncThunk` which auto-generates `pending`, `fulfilled`, and `rejected` action types and handles AbortController-based cancellation.

label: Selector
tooltip: A function that reads and optionally derives data from the Redux store, optionally memoised with Reselect.
definition: A selector is a function that takes the Redux state and returns a derived value. Simple selectors are just arrow functions; complex ones use `createSelector` from Reselect (bundled with Redux Toolkit) to memoize the result — it only recomputes when its inputs change. Selectors decouple components from the store's internal shape: rename a field in state and only the selector changes, not every component that reads it.

label: Redux Middleware
tooltip: A function that intercepts dispatched actions before they reach the reducer — used for async logic, logging, and crash reporting.
definition: Redux middleware is a higher-order function that wraps the `dispatch` function. It sits between `store.dispatch()` and the root reducer, letting you intercept, transform, delay, or side-effect on every action. The standard shape is `(store) => (next) => (action) => { ... }`. `redux-thunk` is the most common — it lets you dispatch functions. `redux-logger` logs state before and after. Multiple middlewares are composed left-to-right.

label: redux-saga
tooltip: A middleware library that manages async side effects using ES6 generator functions and declarative effect descriptors.
definition: redux-saga is a Redux middleware that handles side effects — API calls, WebSocket messages, complex async orchestration — using ES6 generators. Instead of calling async functions directly, sagas `yield` plain effect descriptor objects (`call`, `put`, `take`, `race`, `fork`) that the middleware interprets. Because the generator only produces descriptions and never executes I/O itself, sagas are easy to test without mocks. Key helper effects: `takeEvery` (spawn a task per action), `takeLatest` (cancel previous task on new action), `race` (run effects in parallel, cancel the loser).

label: Flux
tooltip: Facebook's unidirectional data flow architecture — the pattern that directly inspired Redux.
definition: Flux is an application architecture pattern Facebook introduced alongside React in 2014 to tame the complexity of two-way data binding. It enforces a strict one-way cycle: Action → Dispatcher → Store → View. Redux was directly inspired by Flux but simplified it: it eliminates the separate Dispatcher, collapses multiple mutable stores into one immutable state tree, and replaces in-store mutation logic with pure reducer functions. Understanding Flux makes Redux's design decisions (one store, pure reducers, actions as the only mutation path) immediately obvious.

label: Redux Toolkit
tooltip: The official, opinionated Redux toolset — configureStore, createSlice, createAsyncThunk, RTK Query.
definition: Redux Toolkit (RTK) is the official recommended way to write Redux logic. It wraps the raw Redux API with `configureStore` (auto-wires DevTools and thunk middleware), `createSlice` (generates reducers and action creators in one call), `createAsyncThunk` (handles pending/fulfilled/rejected lifecycle actions), and RTK Query (declarative data fetching and caching). It bundles Immer so you can write apparently-mutating reducer logic that actually produces immutable state, and Reselect for memoised selectors.

label: Immer
tooltip: A library that lets you write mutating-looking code that actually produces a new immutable state object.
definition: Immer uses JavaScript `Proxy` to record mutations you make on a draft copy of the state, then produces a new immutable object reflecting those changes — the original is never touched. Redux Toolkit bundles Immer into `createSlice` reducers, so you can write `state.items.push(item)` instead of `return { ...state, items: [...state.items, item] }`. Immer only applies inside `createSlice` (or `createReducer`) — mutating outside those functions is still a bug.

label: Reselect
tooltip: A memoised selector library. createSelector only recomputes when its input selectors return new references.
definition: Reselect is the selector library bundled with Redux Toolkit. Its `createSelector` function takes one or more input selectors and a result function; the result function is only called when the inputs produce new values (by reference equality). This prevents React components from re-rendering when an expensive derived value hasn't actually changed. Selectors compose — pass one `createSelector` output as an input to another to build up a pipeline of cached transformations.

label: combineReducers
tooltip: Utility that merges multiple slice reducers into one root reducer, each responsible for its own state slice.
definition: `combineReducers` (or the object shorthand in `configureStore`) composes multiple reducer functions into a single root reducer. Each slice reducer receives only its own piece of the state tree — it never sees or can accidentally affect sibling slices. On every dispatch, the root reducer calls each slice reducer with its slice and the action, then assembles the results into a new top-level state object. This is the primary mechanism for splitting Redux state by domain without requiring multiple stores.

label: Closure
tooltip: A function that retains access to variables from its outer scope even after that scope has finished executing.
definition: A closure is formed when a function is defined inside another function and the inner function captures (closes over) variables from the outer function's scope. The inner function retains a live reference to those variables — not a copy — so it reads and writes the same memory even after the outer function has returned. Closures are the mechanism behind data privacy (module pattern), partial application, memoization, and any code that needs to 'remember' state between calls without using global variables.

label: Scope
tooltip: The region of code where a variable is accessible. JavaScript has global, function, and block scope.
definition: Scope determines where in the code a variable can be read or written. JavaScript has three scope types: **global scope** (accessible everywhere), **function scope** (`var` declarations are limited to the enclosing function), and **block scope** (`let` and `const` are limited to the nearest `{}`). Scope is lexical — it is determined by where you write the code, not where it is called from. Nested functions form a scope chain: inner scopes can access outer variables, but outer scopes cannot access inner variables.

label: Hoisting
tooltip: JavaScript's behaviour of moving var declarations and function definitions to the top of their scope before execution.
definition: Hoisting is the mechanism by which JavaScript's engine processes declarations before executing code. `var` declarations are hoisted and initialised to `undefined`, so they can be referenced before the line they appear on (returning `undefined`, not an error). Function declarations are fully hoisted — both name and body — so they can be called before their definition. `let` and `const` are hoisted to the top of their block but placed in a Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ) — accessing them before the declaration line throws a `ReferenceError`. Only declarations are hoisted, not assignments.

label: IIFE
tooltip: Immediately Invoked Function Expression — a function that executes the moment it is defined, creating a private scope.
definition: An IIFE (Immediately Invoked Function Expression) is a function expression wrapped in parentheses and immediately called. The wrapping parentheses make it an expression rather than a declaration; the trailing `()` invokes it straight away. IIFEs were the primary way to create private scope before ES6 modules — any `var` inside the IIFE is invisible to the outside world. Today, ES modules provide file-level scope, making IIFEs mostly a legacy pattern, though they still appear in bundled output and libraries that need to support environments without a module system.

label: Event Loop
tooltip: The mechanism that allows JavaScript to perform non-blocking operations by offloading work and processing queued callbacks one at a time.
definition: JavaScript is single-threaded — only one piece of code runs at a time. The event loop is the scheduler that coordinates what runs next. It works with three areas: the **call stack** (currently executing code), the **microtask queue** (Promise callbacks, `queueMicrotask`), and the **macrotask queue** (`setTimeout`, I/O, UI events). After each call stack is emptied, the event loop drains the entire microtask queue first, then picks one macrotask. This ordering is why Promise `.then` callbacks always run before `setTimeout(fn, 0)` callbacks.

label: Promise
tooltip: An object representing the eventual completion or failure of an asynchronous operation, enabling cleaner async code than callbacks.
definition: A Promise is an object that represents the result of an asynchronous operation that will settle at some future point. It has three states: **pending** (initial), **fulfilled** (succeeded with a value), and **rejected** (failed with a reason). Once settled it is immutable. Handlers are registered with `.then(onFulfilled)`, `.catch(onRejected)`, and `.finally(onSettled)`. Each `.then` returns a new Promise, enabling chaining. Promise callbacks are microtasks — they run before the next event loop macrotask. `Promise.all`, `Promise.allSettled`, `Promise.race`, and `Promise.any` coordinate multiple concurrent promises.

label: async / await
tooltip: Syntactic sugar over Promises that makes asynchronous code read like synchronous code.
definition: `async` functions always return a Promise. `await` suspends the function's execution until the awaited Promise settles, then resumes with the resolved value. Under the hood, the engine transforms the async function into a state machine similar to a generator. The suspended function does not block the thread — other tasks continue to run. Error handling uses `try/catch` rather than `.catch()`. Independent async operations should be started simultaneously with `Promise.all` rather than awaited sequentially, to avoid unnecessary latency.

label: Prototype Chain
tooltip: The linked chain of objects JavaScript searches when looking up a property that doesn't exist on the object itself.
definition: Every JavaScript object has an internal `[[Prototype]]` link pointing to another object (or `null`). When you access a property, the engine first checks the object itself. If not found, it follows the `[[Prototype]]` link and checks that object — and so on up the chain until it finds the property or reaches `null` (the chain's end). This is how objects can 'inherit' methods without copying them: they all share a single copy on a prototype object. ES6 `class` and `extends` use this same mechanism.

label: Event Delegation
tooltip: Attaching a single event listener to a parent element to handle events from all its children via bubbling.
definition: Event delegation exploits event bubbling: instead of attaching a listener to every child element, you attach one listener to a common parent. When a child is clicked, the event bubbles up and the parent's handler fires. You use `event.target` (or `event.target.closest(selector)`) to identify which child triggered it. Benefits: fewer listeners (less memory), automatically covers dynamically added children, single cleanup point on teardown. It is especially valuable for large lists, tables, and components that mount/unmount items frequently.

label: Debounce
tooltip: A technique that delays invoking a function until after a specified quiet period since the last call.
definition: Debouncing ensures a function only executes after a specified delay has elapsed since the last invocation. Every new call resets the timer. It is used for events that fire rapidly where you only care about the final settled state — search input (wait until the user stops typing), window resize, autocomplete, form validation. The delay is typically 150–300 ms for user input. A leading variant fires immediately on the first call and then ignores subsequent calls during the quiet period.

label: Throttle
tooltip: A technique that limits a function to fire at most once per specified interval, regardless of how often it is called.
definition: Throttling ensures a function executes at most once per specified time interval, no matter how frequently the triggering event fires. Unlike debounce (which waits for silence), throttle guarantees regular execution during continuous activity. Common use cases: scroll and resize handlers (limit to ~60fps), API rate limiting, game input processing. A leading throttle fires on the first call; a trailing throttle fires after the interval; most implementations fire on both.

label: Generator
tooltip: A function that can pause its execution with yield and resume later, producing a sequence of values on demand.
definition: A generator function (`function*`) returns an iterator when called. Inside the body, `yield` pauses execution and emits a value; calling `.next()` resumes from where it left off. Generators enable lazy evaluation — values are produced only when requested, which is memory-efficient for large or infinite sequences. They also support two-way communication: `yield` expressions can receive values passed via `.next(value)`. Redux-saga uses generators to orchestrate async side effects. `async/await` was itself inspired by the generator + Promise pattern.

label: Symbol
tooltip: A primitive value that is guaranteed to be unique every time it is created, used as collision-free property keys.
definition: Symbol is a primitive type introduced in ES6. Every `Symbol()` call produces a unique value — even if you pass the same description string. Symbols are non-enumerable by default, so they don't appear in `Object.keys()` or `for...in` loops, making them ideal for attaching metadata without polluting the public API. Well-known symbols like `Symbol.iterator`, `Symbol.toPrimitive`, and `Symbol.hasInstance` let objects hook into built-in JavaScript behaviours. `Symbol.for(key)` creates symbols in a global registry shared across modules.

label: Web Worker
tooltip: A background thread in the browser that runs JavaScript without blocking the main UI thread.
definition: Web Workers run JavaScript in a separate thread from the main (UI) thread. Because JavaScript is single-threaded by default, CPU-heavy work blocks the event loop and freezes the UI. Web Workers solve this by offloading computation. Workers communicate with the main thread via `postMessage` / `onmessage` (using the structured-clone algorithm or Transferable objects for zero-copy buffer transfers). Limitations: no DOM access, no `window` or `document`. They can use `fetch`, `IndexedDB`, `WebSocket`, and `WebAssembly`. The `comlink` library wraps workers in a Proxy, eliminating most message-passing boilerplate.

label: Unit Test
tooltip: A test that verifies a single function or component in isolation, with all dependencies replaced by mocks.
definition: A unit test exercises the smallest testable piece of code — typically a single function, method, or component — in complete isolation from external systems. Dependencies such as databases, APIs, and the file system are replaced with mocks or stubs. Unit tests run in milliseconds, are fully deterministic, and pinpoint failures to a specific unit of logic. In JavaScript, Jest is the dominant framework. In React, React Testing Library is used to test component behaviour from the user's perspective without coupling tests to implementation details.

label: Integration Test
tooltip: A test that verifies multiple units work correctly together, often with real (or near-real) dependencies.
definition: Integration tests check the contracts between units — where unit tests guarantee each piece works in isolation, integration tests guarantee they work together. They may use a real database, a real HTTP server, or both. In frontend development, integration tests (using React Testing Library) typically render a feature with real child components but mocked API calls. On the backend, integration tests usually hit a test database seeded with known fixtures. Integration tests are slower than unit tests but catch bugs that only appear at the seams: wrong SQL queries, middleware misconfiguration, broken API contracts.

label: Mock
tooltip: A controlled fake that replaces a real dependency and records calls so you can assert on them.
definition: A mock replaces a real dependency with a controlled substitute that returns predetermined values and records how it was called. Unlike a stub (which only returns values), a mock also lets you assert that your code called it with the right arguments, the right number of times, and in the right order. In Jest, `jest.fn()` creates a mock function and `jest.mock()` replaces an entire module. Mocks are essential for testing code that depends on external systems (databases, APIs, email services) without actually involving them. Over-mocking is a smell — if you mock everything, you end up testing the mocks, not the behaviour.

label: Spy
tooltip: A test double that wraps the real implementation, letting it run while recording calls for later assertion.
definition: A spy wraps the real implementation of a function or method. The original code still executes, but the spy records every call — arguments, return values, and call count — so you can assert on them. This contrasts with a mock, which replaces the real implementation entirely. In Jest, `jest.spyOn(object, 'methodName')` creates a spy. You can optionally override the implementation with `.mockImplementation()`, effectively turning the spy into a mock. Always call `.mockRestore()` after the test to put the original implementation back. Spies are ideal when you want to verify that a collaborator was called without suppressing its real behaviour (e.g., checking a logger was invoked).

label: TDD
tooltip: Test-Driven Development — a practice where you write a failing test before writing the implementation code.
definition: Test-Driven Development (TDD) is a development workflow where you write a failing test first, then write just enough code to make it pass, then refactor — repeating in short cycles. This is often called Red-Green-Refactor. TDD drives API design from the caller's perspective (you write the test before the implementation exists, so you design the API to be easy to use). Benefits include better-designed code, a built-in regression safety net, and tests that document intent. Drawbacks include slower initial velocity, friction with exploratory/UI work, and a tendency toward over-mocking if not applied carefully.

label: Arrange-Act-Assert
tooltip: A pattern for structuring unit tests into three distinct phases: setup, execution, and verification.
definition: Arrange-Act-Assert (AAA) is the standard pattern for structuring tests. Arrange sets up the system under test and its dependencies. Act calls the function or triggers the behaviour being tested — there should be exactly one Act per test. Assert verifies the outcome. The pattern makes tests readable and enforces single responsibility. It maps directly to BDD's Given-When-Then. In React Testing Library: render = Arrange, userEvent/fireEvent = Act, expect = Assert. A test with multiple Acts usually means it's testing more than one thing and should be split.

label: Code Coverage
tooltip: A metric that measures the percentage of your codebase exercised by tests — split into line, branch, and function coverage.
definition: Code coverage measures how much of your source code is executed when tests run. The main types are: line coverage (% of lines executed), branch coverage (% of conditional branches — if/else, ternary — taken), function coverage (% of functions called), and statement coverage (% of statements executed). Branch coverage is the most useful because it catches untested conditional paths. The industry sweet spot is 80–85%. Chasing 100% produces diminishing returns — you end up testing trivial getters and defensive checks. Coverage is a lagging indicator, not a quality metric; a test that achieves 100% coverage without asserting meaningful outcomes is worthless.

label: Test Double
tooltip: An umbrella term for any object that stands in for a real dependency in a test — includes mocks, stubs, spies, fakes, and dummies.
definition: Test double is the umbrella term (coined by Gerard Meszaros) for any object that replaces a real dependency in a test. The five subtypes are: Dummy (passed but never used — fills a parameter list), Stub (returns hardcoded values), Mock (records interactions and can assert on them), Spy (wraps real implementation, records calls), and Fake (a working simplified implementation — e.g. an in-memory database). In everyday JavaScript/TypeScript usage the terms mock and stub are often used loosely to mean any test double, but understanding the distinctions helps you choose the right tool.

label: Singleton
tooltip: A creational pattern that ensures a class has only one instance and provides a global access point to it.
definition: The Singleton pattern restricts instantiation of a class to a single object. In JavaScript, ES module exports are natural singletons — every import returns the same module-level object. Common uses: a Redux store, a Supabase client, an app-wide logger. Singletons can be problematic in tests because they carry state between tests and can't be easily replaced with mocks. Prefer dependency injection over ambient singletons when testability matters.

label: Observer
tooltip: A behavioral pattern where a subject notifies all subscribed observers automatically when its state changes.
definition: The Observer pattern defines a one-to-many dependency between objects. When the subject (publisher) changes state, all registered observers (subscribers) are notified. It is the foundation of event-driven programming. In the browser: `addEventListener` is the Observer pattern. In Node.js: `EventEmitter`. In React: the Context API re-renders consumers when context value changes; Zustand re-renders components subscribed to a state slice. The key benefit is decoupling — the subject doesn't need to know anything about its observers beyond the notification interface.

label: Strategy
tooltip: A behavioral pattern that defines a family of interchangeable algorithms and lets you swap them at runtime.
definition: The Strategy pattern encapsulates a family of algorithms behind a common interface, making them interchangeable without modifying the context that uses them. This eliminates long if/else or switch chains and follows the Open/Closed Principle — adding a new algorithm means adding a new strategy, not editing existing code. In JavaScript, strategies are often plain functions stored in a map. In React, custom hooks that accept a strategy function (a sort function, a validation function) are the idiomatic form.

label: Decorator
tooltip: A structural pattern that wraps an object to add behaviour without modifying the original class.
definition: The Decorator pattern attaches additional responsibilities to an object dynamically by wrapping it in another object with the same interface. It is an alternative to subclassing and follows the Open/Closed Principle. In JavaScript, Higher-Order Functions are functional decorators. In React, Higher-Order Components (HOCs) like `withAuth()` and `withErrorBoundary()` are classic decorators — they wrap a component and return an enhanced version. The TC39 decorators proposal (`@decorator`) brings the pattern to class syntax.

label: Facade
tooltip: A structural pattern that provides a simplified interface to a complex subsystem.
definition: The Facade pattern hides the complexity of a subsystem behind a clean, simple API. Callers interact with the facade rather than coordinating multiple low-level components themselves. In frontend, API service layers are classic facades — `authService.login()` hides fetch calls, token storage, header management, and error normalisation. Custom hooks that wrap TanStack Query (e.g. `useProducts()`) are facades that hide query keys, cache config, and data transformation. Facades don't add new capabilities — they simplify access to existing ones.

label: Adapter
tooltip: A structural pattern that converts one interface into another that clients expect, making incompatible interfaces work together.
definition: The Adapter pattern wraps an object with an incompatible interface and exposes the interface clients expect — like a power adapter for electrical sockets. In frontend, adapters normalise third-party API responses into the shape your app uses, wrap a library being replaced (so call sites don't need to change), or unify data from multiple sources into a consistent format. Adapters are distinct from facades: a facade simplifies complexity inside your system; an adapter translates an external interface into your system's expected shape.

label: Dependency Injection
tooltip: A technique where a class receives its dependencies from the outside rather than creating them itself.
definition: Dependency Injection (DI) is a technique where dependencies are passed to a class or function rather than created internally. This makes the dependency explicit (visible in the function signature), easy to swap (pass a mock in tests), and decoupled (the class doesn't know or care which concrete implementation it gets). In React, DI is idiomatic: props inject dependencies into components, Context provides them to subtrees, and custom hooks can accept repositories/services as arguments. DI is the preferred alternative to the Service Locator pattern, which hides dependencies behind a global registry.

label: Design Pattern
tooltip: A named, reusable solution to a commonly recurring problem in software design.
definition: Design patterns are battle-tested, named templates for solving recurring software design problems. They originate from the Gang of Four (GoF) book *Design Patterns* (1994), which catalogued 23 patterns in three categories: Creational (how objects are created — Singleton, Factory, Builder), Structural (how objects are composed — Adapter, Facade, Decorator, Proxy, Composite), and Behavioral (how objects communicate — Observer, Strategy, Command, State). Patterns give teams a shared vocabulary and encode decades of collective design experience. They are templates — not code to copy. Over-applying patterns where simpler solutions exist is a common mistake.
